objectives: Connect to NLP tokenization + morpheme analysis.

slides.title: Morphemes: minimal units of meaning
slides.body:
**Morpheme** = smallest unit carrying meaning or grammatical function.

**English example**: 'unhappiness' = un- + happy + -ness. Three morphemes.

Two main types of morphological process:
• **Derivational**: creates new words. 'happy' (adj) → 'happiness' (noun). Often changes category.
• **Inflectional**: marks grammatical relations (tense, number, case, gender, person). 'walk' → 'walked' (past tense). Same lemma.

**Affixes** (bound morphemes):
• **Prefix**: pre-fix (English un-, re-, pre-).
• **Suffix**: suf-fix (English -ness, -tion, -ed, -s).
• **Infix**: inside the root (Tagalog -um-, English 'abso-fucking-lutely' = expletive infix).
• **Circumfix**: wraps the root (German ge...-t past participle: ge-spiel-t).
• **Reduplication**: copy stem (Tagalog: bili 'buy' → bibili 'will buy').

**Bound vs free morphemes**: 'happy' is free (stands alone); '-ness' is bound. Languages vary in proportion.

**Cumulative morphs vs agglutinative**:
- Cumulative (fusional, Latin): single morph carries many features. Latin '-orum' = genitive + plural + masculine.
- Agglutinative (Turkish, Finnish): one morph per feature, transparent. Turkish 'evlerimde' = ev (house) + ler (plural) + im (my) + de (locative).

slides.title: Morphological typology
slides.body:
Languages span a spectrum of morphological complexity:

1. **Isolating / analytic** (Mandarin, Vietnamese, modern English): little inflection; grammatical relations via word order + particles. Vocabulary ratio of morphemes per word ~1.
   - Mandarin 我吃苹果 'I eat apple' = wo (I) chi (eat) ping-guo (apple).
   - English: 'I will go to the store tomorrow.' No verb inflection except 3sg + past.

2. **Agglutinative** (Turkish, Finnish, Japanese, Swahili, Quechua, Korean): many morphs per word; transparent boundaries.
   - Turkish 'evlerimizde' = ev (house) + ler (plural) + imiz (our) + de (in) = 'in our houses.'
   - Finnish 'taloihinsa' = talo + i + hin + sa = 'into their houses.'

3. **Fusional / inflecting** (Latin, Russian, Sanskrit, modern Romance): morphs encode multiple features; boundaries opaque.
   - Latin 'amō, amās, amat, amāmus, amātis, amant' = 'I love, you sg love, he loves, we love, you pl love, they love.' Person + number + tense fused.
   - Russian: rich case system (6 cases × 3 genders).

4. **Polysynthetic** (Inuktitut, Cherokee, Mohawk, Greenlandic, Chukchi): extremely complex; whole sentences encoded in single words.
   - Greenlandic 'tusaa-nngit-su-usaar-tuaannar-sinnaa-nngi-vip-pu-tit' = 'You can't pretend to not be hearing all the time.' (Loosely.)
   - Often noun incorporation (object embedded in verb).

**Index of synthesis** (Greenberg 1960): morphemes/word ratio. Isolating ~1.0; English ~1.5; Russian ~3; Sanskrit ~3.5; Turkish ~3.5; Inuktitut ~5+.

**Cross-cutting**: agglutinative vs fusional are orthogonal to synthetic-vs-isolating; describe how clearly affixes can be segmented.

Most languages mixed; English is mostly analytic (lost most Old English inflection) but retains some fusional (he-she pronouns, irregular plurals, irregular past). Pure types are theoretical extremes.

slides.title: Modern morphological theory + NLP
slides.body:
**Morpheme-based vs word-based** approaches:
- Morphemes are theoretical units; sometimes contested whether they exist as such.
- Word-and-paradigm models: treat words as wholes within paradigms (rows × columns of person/number/tense).
- Frequency + analogy + neural network models challenge strict morphological decomposition.

**Morphophonology**: phonological rules interacting with morphology.
- English plural /-z/ → [s] / voiceless _ (cats); [z] / voiced V_ (dogs); [əz] / sibilant _ (foxes).
- Vowel harmony in Turkish, Finnish: suffix vowels match root vowel (front/back, rounded/unrounded).
- Umlaut in Germanic: pluralization via vowel alternation (foot/feet).

**Allomorphy**: phonological + lexical variants of one morpheme.
- 'in-' negation: 'inactive', 'illegal', 'irregular', 'impossible' — assimilation.
- Suppletion: completely different forms (go/went; good/better/best).

**Morphological productivity**: how readily new words coined.
- Productive: '-ness' (newness, busyness, OKness).
- Non-productive: '-th' in 'warmth, length' but not '*newth.'
- Borrowings + neologisms (selfie, vape, doomscroll).

**Computational morphology**:
- **Finite-state morphology** (Beesley + Karttunen 2003): FST-based morphological analyzers + generators. Used in: Apple keyboards (Inuktitut), Google search expansion, Helsinki Finite-State Toolkit.
- **Two-level morphology** (Koskenniemi 1983): rules align surface + lexical levels.
- **Stemming + lemmatization**: NLP pipeline. Porter stemmer (English heuristic); WordNet lemmatizer; spaCy + Stanford pipelines.
- **Subword tokenization** (modern NLP): BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece. Don't claim to be linguistic morphology but capture useful regularities. GPT-3 uses ~50k BPE tokens.
- **Morpheme-aware embeddings**: explore linguistic structure in vector space. BERT + variants implicit.
- **Low-resource languages**: morphology critical for languages with little training data; rule-based analyzers + multilingual transfer.

question.question: Analyze Turkish word morphology
question.goal: Decompose the Turkish word 'evlerimizden' (= 'from our houses') into morphemes + identify each.

steps.reveal: **-ler** = plural marker (vowel-harmony variant: -lar after back vowels, -ler after front vowels). Here 'ev' has front 'e' so -ler.
**-imiz** = 1pl possessive ('our'). Cross-linguistic agglutinative possessive marking on noun.
**-den** = ablative case ('from'). Vowel-harmony variant: -dan / -den / -tan / -ten based on root vowels + voicing.

**4 morphemes**: ev + -ler + -imiz + -den. Index of synthesis = 4 (way above English ~1.5). Transparent agglutinative structure: each affix has clear function + boundary. Compare English 'from our houses' = 4 separate words; Turkish encodes same information in single word.

This is why finite-state morphology + careful tokenization matter for Turkish NLP — naive word-level tokenization loses huge structure. Modern NLP uses subword (BPE) which captures regularities without explicit morphology.

question.question: Order these languages by morphological complexity (index of synthesis: isolating → polysynthetic).
question.explanation:
Morphological-complexity hierarchy (rough morphemes/word index):
• **Mandarin**: ~1.0 — analytic/isolating. Almost no inflection; grammar via word order + particles + classifier nouns.
• **English**: ~1.5 — mostly analytic but retains some inflection (plural -s, past -ed, comparative -er, possessive -'s, person-number on verbs). Heavily reduced from Old English.
• **Russian**: ~3.0 — fusional (Slavic family). Rich case + gender + aspect system in compact suffixes.
• **Turkish**: ~3.5 — agglutinative. Multiple transparent suffixes per noun + verb.
• **Inuktitut / Greenlandic**: ~5+ — polysynthetic. Verbal + nominal incorporation; whole-sentence-as-word.

This is a useful theoretical scale but real languages mix types. Languages drift along the cline over centuries — Latin (fusional) → Romance (less fusional). English lost inflection from OE; Mandarin lost some from Old Chinese. Polysynthetic vs isolating not a developmental hierarchy — all stable + adequate; reflect different historical + areal pressures.

question.question: Classify each English suffix as DERIVATIONAL or INFLECTIONAL.

bins.label: Derivational (changes category or creates new word)

question.explanation:
Derivational vs inflectional in English (English has just a few inflectional suffixes; most are derivational):
• **Derivational**: -ness (adj→noun), -tion (verb→noun), -ly (adj→adv), -able (verb→adj), agent -er (verb→noun: writer). Changes category or meaning.
• **Inflectional**: -s (plural), -ed (past), -ing (progressive), -s (3sg present), -er (comparative on adj), -est (superlative), -'s (possessive). Marks grammatical relations within paradigm.

Note two -er suffixes: agent ('writer' = person who writes) is derivational; comparative ('bigger' = more big) is inflectional. Homographic but functionally distinct.

Modern English has only ~8-10 inflectional suffixes (compared to ~50+ in Old English; ~100+ in Sanskrit). English drifted toward isolating typology over 1500 years.

question.question: Why has Modern English lost most of the inflectional morphology Old English had?
options: Multiple factors: (1) phonological erosion of unstressed final syllables (over centuries); (2) contact with Norse (1000-1100 CE) + Norman French (1066+) creating intermediate-fluency-driven simplification; (3) reliance on word order + prepositions shifted; (4) loss of grammatical gender + case happened gradually 1100-1450. End result: ~8-10 inflectional suffixes, compared to ~50+ in Old English. This is the path from synthetic to analytic typology + happens to languages with extensive contact + non-native-speaker simplification pressure.
question.explanation:
**Old English → Modern English morphological loss**:

*Old English (~700-1100 CE)*:
- Rich inflection: 4 cases (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative) × 3 genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) × strong/weak adjective paradigms.
- Verbs: 7 strong-verb classes + weak verbs; subjunctive vs indicative; multiple person + number forms.
- Synthetic/fusional typology; close to other Germanic languages.

*Decline (1100-1450 CE)*:

1. **Phonological erosion**: unstressed vowel endings (-e, -a, -u) merged + reduced to schwa, then disappeared. 'stānes' → 'stones' lost the genitive distinction over centuries.

2. **Norse contact** (8th-11th century): Vikings settled extensive Danelaw; intermarriage. Old Norse + Old English shared roots but had different inflections → ambiguity → contact-induced simplification. Possible role of pidginization between adult bilinguals.

3. **Norman conquest 1066**: French superstrate. Sustained French rule for ~300 years (with all formal + written language). English became 'low' register; vocabulary borrowed (~40% of modern English from French + Latin); native simplified.

4. **Word-order rigidification**: as inflection eroded, English shifted to fixed SVO word order to maintain comprehension.

5. **Loss of grammatical gender**: by ~1250.

6. **Loss of case system**: dative + accusative merged → nominative vs oblique; case lost on nouns by ~1400; preserved only on pronouns (he/him/his).

7. **Strong/weak verb distinction**: many strong verbs regularized to weak (-ed). 'help/holp/holpen' → 'help/helped/helped' over centuries.

*Modern English inflection*:
- Noun: -s plural, -'s possessive. (Compare Sanskrit ~8 case forms × 3 numbers × 3 genders.)
- Verb: -s (3sg present), -ed (past), -ing (progressive), -en (past participle, irregular). And modal auxiliaries do the rest.
- Adjective: -er (comparative), -est (superlative). No agreement with noun.
- Pronouns: 3 cases (I/me/my, he/him/his, she/her/hers, etc.).

*Cross-linguistic comparison*:
- French: lost much of Latin inflection but kept ~6-8 verb tense/mood forms × 6 person/number.
- German: kept more cases (4) + gender; more synthetic than English.
- Scandinavian: lost gender + cases similar to English; reduced verb inflection.
- Romance + Slavic + Greek: retained extensive inflection.

*Why this matters for NLP*:
- Morphologically poor English easier to model with shallow methods (BoW, n-grams).
- Morphologically rich languages (Russian, Turkish, Finnish) benefit from morphological awareness or subword tokenization (BPE; many modern NLP systems use SentencePiece).
- Low-resource languages: morphology is often the bottleneck — limited data + complex morphology.

*Theoretical models*:
- **Pidginization / creolization** as agent of simplification (Trudgill 2009).
- **Sapir's drift** (1921): languages have systematic tendencies toward certain typological shifts.
- **Imperfect L2 acquisition + lifelong contact** drive specific simplification patterns.

Language change is one of the most active areas of linguistics + has cognitive + sociological + historical dimensions all together.

hints: What's the path of typological change?
slides.workedSolution: Old English (700-1100) had rich Germanic inflection (4 cases × 3 genders × strong/weak adj/verb). Decline 1100-1450 from: phonological erosion of unstressed endings; Norse contact (Vikings, pidginization); Norman conquest 1066 with French superstrate ~300 yr; loss of grammatical gender ~1250; loss of case ~1400; strong verbs regularized. Modern English: ~10 inflectional suffixes, mostly analytic with fixed word order + auxiliary verbs. Contrast: French/German kept more; Russian/Sanskrit very synthetic. NLP implication: English shallow; morphology-rich languages need subword tokenization or morphological analyzers.

question.question: Turkish 'evlerimizde' = ev + ler + imiz + de. How many morphemes in this word?
question.hint: Count: ev (root) + ler (plural) + imiz (our) + de (locative) = 4 morphemes.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how morphological structure affects subword tokenization in modern NLP (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece).
question.rubric: Mentions: morphologically complex languages (Turkish, Finnish, Inuktitut) produce many word forms from same root + affixes. Naive word-level tokenization → enormous vocabulary + many rare tokens. Subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) breaks words into sub-units based on frequency, capturing morphology indirectly. For English: 'unhappy' → 'un', 'happy' may be discovered. For Turkish: 'evlerimizde' → likely 'ev', 'ler', 'imiz', 'de' (transparent agglutinative). Trade-offs: smaller vocabulary (~30-50k vs millions); generalizes to unseen forms; captures regularities without explicit morphology. Limits: doesn't always align with linguistic morphemes; can split arbitrarily; allomorphy + suppletion not captured. Modern systems (LLMs): mostly use BPE/SentencePiece. Specialized: morpheme-aware tokenizers (Trankit, UDPipe) for morphology-rich + low-resource. Closes: subword tokenization is engineering compromise that works well in practice for many languages but linguistic morphology still relevant + improves low-resource NLP.
